title: House Robber - one best-so-far per house instead of re-branching

dp: take, skip = skip + money, max(take, skip)

frames.intro: each house is a rob-or-skip choice; robbing one blocks its neighbor.
frames.invariant: you can never take two houses that sit next to each other.
frames.note: The houses in a row, each holding some money. You cannot rob two adjacent houses. We want the largest total.
At each house you either ROB it (take its money, then you must skip the next) or SKIP it. best(i) = max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + money). Naive recursion re-solves the same best(i) in many branches.

frames.intro: one running best per house, each computed once left to right.
frames.invariant: best[i] = most money robbable from houses 0..i.
frames.note: Start with nothing taken. best[i] compares skipping house i (keep best[i-1]) against robbing it (best[i-2] + money[i]).
House 0 ($2): rob = best[-2] 0 + 2 = 2 vs skip = best[-1] 0. best[0] = 2.
House 1 ($7): rob = best[-1] 0 + 7 = 7 vs skip = best[0] 2. best[1] = 7.
House 2 ($9): rob = best[0] 2 + 9 = 11 vs skip = best[1] 7. best[2] = 11.
House 3 ($3): rob = best[1] 7 + 3 = 10 vs skip = best[2] 11. best[3] = 11.
House 4 ($1): rob = best[2] 11 + 1 = 12 vs skip = best[3] 11. best[4] = 12.

frames.intro: the last house's best already folded in every earlier choice.
frames.note: best[4] = 12 — that plan robs houses 0, 2, 4 (2 + 9 + 1). No two are neighbors.
Edge case: one house holding 5. Nothing to conflict with, so rob it — the answer is 5.
